source_read: PDF of scanned print pages, Addiction 91(12), pp. 1765-1772 (all pages; poor text layer, so every number was read on pages rendered at 150 and 300 dpi)

claims.overstatement: The Michigan sentence is accurate and correctly labelled second-hand. Two points for the claim's closing sentences, as far as this source goes: (1) 'none compares post-mortem levels with levels in living people who use the drugs outside treatment' should allow that this review relays, without figures, three studies that compared fatal cases with survivors of overdose (one of them, by its title in the reference list, measured serum morphine in living people who use heroin); suggested: 'none of the studies read here made such a comparison itself'. (2) The review does not say who classified Monforte's deaths or whether the levels were known, so 'the people who decided the cause of death knew the measured levels' is not supported by this source.
claims.note: Monforte (1977) is placed in Michigan by the review's contaminants section (quinine in 57% of cases in Michigan, p. 1767). The comparison group is described only as a similar group of people who used heroin and died of other causes such as trauma or homicide; its size, the specimen and how 'no higher than' was judged are not given. The review also notes that blood morphine depends on route, amount, body weight, time since the last dose and individual pharmacokinetics (p. 1766), and that very little is known about blood morphine in living intoxicated people (p. 1769).

anchors.locator: Mechanisms of heroin-caused deaths > True overdose, paragraph 1 (continues into right column); Contaminants, paragraph 1
anchors.extracted: Morphine levels where reported are skewed to the low end; Monforte (1977) found 74% of fatal heroin overdose cases had blood levels no higher than a similar group of people who used heroin and died of other causes (e.g. trauma, homicide); the same series is placed in Michigan (quinine in 57% of cases).

A third of the authors' NSW series had morphine below 0.16 mg/L, the laboratories' toxic level for people without opioid tolerance; many fatal cases said to have levels no higher than survivors of overdose, citing three studies without figures.

anchors.locator: Is the term 'overdose' a misnomer?, paragraph 1
anchors.extracted: In a substantial share of cases blood morphine alone cannot account for the death; many cases have levels at the low end, or no higher than survivors or people dependent on heroin who die of other causes; heroin may often be no more than contributory.
Very little information on blood morphine in living intoxicated people who use heroin; comparing them with fatal cases is named as a research need.
Blood morphine depends on route, amount, body weight, time since the last dose and individual pharmacokinetics.

claims.overstatement: Every figure from this review reproduces. Not supported as attributed: the sentence 'but finding other drugs does not show that they caused the death, the comparison with survivors rests on three studies cited without figures, tolerance was measured in no study, and low morphine can also reflect a death hours after the last injection ... or change after death (Darke & Zador, 1996)' cites the review for the editors' critique. The review supports only the descriptive parts (three studies without figures, p. 1767; no tolerance measure anywhere; morphine depends on time since the last dose, p. 1766, and many deaths take hours, p. 1767); it argues the opposite about other drugs (that they contribute causally) and never mentions change after death. Label these as the editors' reading or move the citation. Smaller points: the 12% for benzodiazepines is diazepam only (Monforte 1977); the claim quotes this source twice (the minority phrase, exact on p. 1770, and the proposed term), against the one-quotation rule; the term can stand without quotation marks.
claims.note: Counts recomputed on the page: morphine only in six studies, 23, 27, 35, 38, 40 and 48%; alcohol in 13 studies, 29-75% (68% and 74% each from two studies); mean blood alcohol 0.09, 0.10, 0.14 and 0.16 g/100 mL; benzodiazepines in four studies, 12 (diazepam), 22, 27 and 55%; morphine lower with alcohol in five cited studies (median 0.17 against 0.34 mg/L in the authors' series; r = -0.14 among 505 alcohol-positive deaths; r = -0.28 in the authors' series); instant 14% and over 3 h 22% (authors' series), over 3 h 52%, over 2 h 44%; others present 58, 61 and 79%, and over half without a figure. Not in the claim but relevant: only 23% collapsed immediately after injection in a US army series, and in the authors' series medical help was sought before death in only 10%. The review's NSW series (152 deaths in 1992) is Zador, Sunjic & Darke (1996), co-authored by the first author. No methods section, no search, no appraisal; cited sources run from 1967 to 1996. Citation slips in the review (Zador 1995 and Kintz 1995 in the text, 1996 and 1989 in the list) do not affect the figures.

anchors.extracted: Review of the literature on deaths attributed to heroin overdose: deaths with heroin alone appear a minority, other depressants (alcohol, benzodiazepines) commonly detected; deaths attributed to overdose likely to have morphine no higher than survivors or people who use heroin and die of other causes; the term overdose called misleading in many cases.

anchors.locator: A new perspective: polydrug use theory, paragraph 2
anchors.extracted: Morphine the only drug detected at autopsy in 23% (Monforte 1977), 27% (Zador et al. 1996), 35% (Richards 1976), 38% (Wahbah 1993), 40% (Steentoft 1988) and 48% (Nakamura 1978) of deaths: six studies, 23-48%.

Alcohol positive at autopsy in 29, 31, 34, 40, 45 (authors' series), 47, 48, 50, 68 (two studies), 74 (two studies) and 75% of deaths attributed to overdose: 29-75% across 13 studies (editors' count); mean blood alcohol 0.09, 0.10, 0.14 and 0.16 g/100 mL where reported; 22% of the authors' series above 0.20 g/100 mL.

Morphine lower when alcohol present in five cited studies, clinical significance called unclear: authors' series median 0.17 against 0.34 mg/L in morphine-only cases (significant); means 0.43 against 0.52 mg/L; medians 0.4 against 0.7 micromol/kg and 0.4 against 0.6 mg/L; correlation of blood alcohol with blood morphine r = -0.14 in 505 alcohol-positive deaths and r = -0.28 in the authors' series.
Benzodiazepines at autopsy: diazepam in 12% (Monforte 1977), benzodiazepines in 55% of a Swedish sample, 27% of the authors' series and 22% (Richards 1976).

Overdose defined classically as an amount or purity beyond current tolerance (tolerance not measured); a third of the authors' series below 0.16 mg/L (the laboratories' toxic level for people without tolerance); 74% of one 1977 series no higher than people who used heroin and died of other causes; levels no higher than survivors asserted from three studies without figures.

anchors.locator: Circumstances of fatalities attributed to overdose, paragraph 3
anchors.extracted: Instant death not the norm: 23% collapsed immediately (Manning 1983); 14% instant and 22% over 3 h (authors' series); over 3 h in 52% (Garriot & Sturner 1973); over 2 h in 44% (Nakamura 1978); instant deaths rare in Monforte (no figures).

anchors.locator: Circumstances of fatalities attributed to overdose, paragraph 2
anchors.extracted: Others present at the death in 58% (authors' series), 61% (Walsh 1991), 79% (Drew 1982) and over half, without a figure (Manning 1983).

anchors.locator: Circumstances of fatalities attributed to overdose, paragraph 4
anchors.extracted: Help sought only 3 h after the final injection in 42% (Manning 1983); in the authors' series medical help was sought before death in only 10% and there was no intervention in 79%.

Quinine found in 19% (New York) and 57% (Michigan) but at autopsy levels within therapeutic range; no contaminants in the authors' 152 deaths; pulmonary oedema non-specific: other mechanisms judged minor.

anchors.locator: Is the term 'overdose' a misnomer?, paragraph 1; Conclusions, paragraphs 1-2
anchors.extracted: Blood morphine alone cannot account for many deaths; heroin perhaps only contributory in many; the term overdose may apply correctly to only a minority of heroin-related deaths; the authors propose terms such as multiple drug toxicity.

Official statistics record cause of death only as due to opiates, without the type of opiate or whether several drugs were detected; the authors suggest recording morphine only, heroin with alcohol, and so on.

Blood morphine depends on route, amount, body weight, time since the last dose and individual pharmacokinetics (the basis for reading low morphine as possibly a late death; the review does not draw that inference or mention post-mortem change).

key_findings.correction: Same six values found in step 1.

reporting_issues.note: Confirmed on the rendered pages: Kintz 1995 and Drew 1983 in the text (p. 1767) against 1989 and 1982 in the list.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with high overall: no search or appraisal, weighted to the authors' own series, and alternative explanations for low morphine (delayed death, redistribution, tolerance) not weighed.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right: presence of other drugs and low morphine are read as causal contribution, and the survivor comparison in the abstract rests on three studies without figures.

missed: p. 1770, reference list: by its title, Aderjan et al. (1995), one of the three studies cited for morphine no higher than in survivors, compared serum morphine in living people who use heroin with heroin-related deaths. The card rightly notes that the comparison is cited without figures; it could add that one cited study did sample living people, which bears on cl_gen_deaths_level_cause's statement that none of the studies compares post-mortem levels with levels in living people outside treatment.
